To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants is associated with a significant reduction in the number of circulating FHT-like CD4+ cells in patients with SLE.
the administration of steroids to SLE patients reduces the number of circulating FhlCD4+ T cells.

(1) The prevalence of FHT-like CD4 T cell is higher in active SLE patients, and (2) The FHT-like CD14 T cells in active SLE are associated with disease activity and the expression of the B cell activating factor (BAFF).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of steroid hormones on the immune system.
the effects of the glucocorticoid receptor on T cells, and in particular, on the generation of follicular helper T (Tfh) cells.
the study of the role of the CD4 + CD25 + Foxp3 + Treg cell population in the pathogenesis of SLE.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of corticosteroids is not a risk factor for the development of diabetes in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, and the use of cortisone is associated with a lower risk of developing diabetes in patients with systemic sclerosis.
steroids are beneficial to patients with systemic lupers erythematosus (SLE) but they are associated with increased risk of infections, diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, cataracts, and glaucoma.
steroids have a significant effect on CD4(+) T cell subsets, but not on the CD19(+) B cell subset, in patients with SLE, which might be related to the immunosuppressive effect of steroids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

steroids are associated with a decrease in the circulating follicular helper cell like (Tfh)-like cells, but not in the circulating Tfh cells, which is associated with a decrease of the disease activity.
we have demonstrated the presence of circulating follicular helper CD4+ T cell-like (Tfh-like) cells in patients with SLE.

we have demonstrated that circulating follicular helper CD4+ T cell-like cells (TFH-like) are increased in patients with systemic Lupus erythematosu (SLE), and that this increase in TFH-like cells is associated with increased levels of autoantibodies, and that steroids reduce TFH-like cell numbers and autoantibody titres in SLE.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we found that the number of circulating CD4+ T follicular helper (Tfh) cells was higher in SLE patients and correlated with disease activity.
the effects of steroids on circulating FHT cells are not uniform across all SLE patients.
the effects of corticosteroids on circulating follicular T helper cells are more complex than previously thought.
